content: <thought>We have the mass spectrum showing a molecular ion at m/z ≈199 Da, with an M+1 peak (~9 % of M) indicating roughly 8–9 carbons. The strong peak at m/z ≈201 (intensity ~98 %) suggests the true molecular ion is at 201 Da and the 199 Da peak is an M‑2 isotope (e.g., due to two 13C atoms). A formula that fits 201 Da with ~9 carbons is C₁₀H₁₃NO₂ (exact mass 199.0946) – not matching. Trying C₁₁H₁₅NO₂ (exact mass 197.1103) – no. A better match is C₁₁H₁₃NO₂ (exact mass 191.0946) – still off. Considering a bromine atom (≈79.9 Da) would give an M+2 pattern of ~1:1, which we do not see. The isotopic pattern is more consistent with a molecule containing one chlorine (≈35.45 Da) giving M and M+2 peaks at ~3:1, also not observed. Therefore the most plausible explanation is that the molecular ion is at 201 Da, corresponding to a formula like C₁₁H₁₅O₃ (exact mass 199.099 Da) plus a proton (M+H⁺ = 200). However, without additional NMR data we cannot uniquely assign the structure. The next logical step is to obtain the ¹H NMR spectrum to narrow down functional groups and substitution patterns.
